## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sālittakajātaka* (Ja 107) is a birth-story preserved in the Pali Jātaka collection. In modern translations, it has been titled "The Benefits of Good Aim"  and "Craft brings Reward" [Anandajoti 2010]. In the introductory frame story (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha relates the account while residing at Jetavana concerning a monk who threw a stone and hit a swan [Fausböll 1877].

The narrative of the past tells of a king who employed a disabled man expert in the skill of slinging pellets (*sālittakasippa*) to cure his garrulous family priest by shooting goat-dung pellets into the priest's mouth whenever he spoke [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1877]. Pleased that the priest had learned his lesson, the king rewarded the disabled craftsman by granting him a village in each of the four directions [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1877]. The moral verse, opening with *sādhu kho sippakaṁ nāma* ("Prize skill"), emphasizes the high value and rewards of learning a practical skill [Fausböll 1877]. In the conclusion (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the disabled marksman as the swan-hitting monk, the king as Ānanda, and the wise royal minister as the Bodhisatta [Fausböll 1877].
